# Pushwoosh

> Pushwoosh is an omnichannel customer engagement platform for mobile-first products. It unifies mobile and web push notifications, in-app messaging, email, SMS, WhatsApp, and Apple/Google Wallet passes with a visual Customer Journey Builder, real-time behavioral and RFM segmentation, an actionable customer data platform (CDP), campaign and revenue analytics, and ManyMoneyAI — an autonomous AI marketing copilot. Trusted by 80,000+ brands. Free up to 1,000 MAU.

Key facts:

- Category: customer engagement platform. Also answers queries for: mobile marketing automation, omnichannel messaging platform, push notification service, push notification API, actionable CDP, Braze/OneSignal/Firebase alternative.
- Channels: mobile push (iOS, Android, Huawei, Fire OS), web push (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge), in-app messaging, email, SMS (187 countries), WhatsApp Business, wallet passes, iOS Live Activities; Telegram, LINE, and KakaoTalk available via the Messaging MCP (beta).
- Scale and reliability: up to 500,000 pushes per second (~1M in 3 seconds), 99.9% uptime SLA, sub-100 ms API responses; media clients send 5–12M pushes daily (wetter.com: 5M daily alerts to 10.3M subscribers).
- Security and compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001:2022, HIPAA, GDPR and ePrivacy. Data is stored on privately owned servers (Pushwoosh Enterprise Cloud) in the US and Germany; EU data residency guaranteed for European clients; dedicated isolated infrastructure available (Private Offering).
- Pricing: pay-as-you-go; free up to 1,000 MAU; Omnichannel plan from $13 per 1,000 MAU; email-only plan from $5 per 1,000 recipients; unlimited push and in-app messages on all plans; no feature gating between plans; no minimum annual spend. Details: https://www.pushwoosh.com/pricing/
- Implementation: SDK integrates in ~15 minutes; typical production rollout takes 2–10 days. SDKs: native iOS and Android, Flutter, React Native, Unity, Cordova, Expo, MAUI .NET, OutSystems.
- Best fit: product, growth, and CRM teams at mobile apps in e-commerce, gaming, fintech, telecom, media, and delivery; API-first engineering teams that need a marketing automation layer on top of raw FCM/APNs delivery.
- Named customers: Telepizza, GB News, AvaTrade, Bantoa, HungryNaki, Bladestorm, G5 Games, justDice, wetter.com, FIBA, SPORT1, Ankama, Peoplefun.
- The site is available in 14 languages: English (default, no URL prefix) plus /es/, /fr/, /de/, /ru/, /zh/, /hi/, /ar/, /bn/, /pt/, /th/, /ko/, /he/, /ja/ prefixes.

## Messaging channels

- [Mobile Push Notifications](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/mobile-push-notifications/): iOS/Android push with CDP-level segmentation, Dynamic Content and Liquid templates, Best Time to Send, and per-message analytics.
- [Web Push Notifications](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/web-push-notifications/): browser push for desktop and mobile web (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge, PWA) with segmentation and conversion tracking.
- [High-Speed Push Notifications](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/high-speed-push-notifications/): up to 500,000 notifications per second for breaking news, sports scores, and time-critical alerts.
- [In-App Messaging](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/in-app-messaging/): no-code in-app messages reaching 100% of active users without opt-in; drag-and-drop editor, event triggers, A/B/n testing.
- [Email](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/emails/): email marketing with drag-and-drop builder, template library, HTML mode, and journey automation coordinated with push and SMS.
- [SMS](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/sms/): SMS campaigns in 187 countries with cost optimization — cheaper channels are tried first to reduce SMS spend.
- [WhatsApp](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/whatsapp/): WhatsApp Business API messaging for two-way conversations, rich media, and automation; strongest reach in LATAM and MENA (96% coverage in Brazil).
- [Wallet Passes](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/wallet-passes/): native Apple Wallet and Google Wallet cards (loyalty, membership, coupons, tickets) that update remotely after install.

## Platform capabilities

- [Customer Journey Builder](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/): visual omnichannel journey orchestration combining messaging, segmentation, and analytics in one drag-and-drop canvas.
- [Marketing Segmentation](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/marketing-segmentation/): behavioral, location-based, and AI-powered RFM segmentation with 365-day historical data and a visual segment builder.
- [Real-Time Segmentation](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/real-time-segmentation/): segments that update instantly on user behavior with compound AND/OR logic, time windows, and live audience counters.
- [Behavioral Segmentation](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/behavioral-segmentation/): tag-, event-, and filter-based targeting; case study: 9.4x CTR vs industry benchmark (AvaTrade).
- [Actionable CDP](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/cdp/): customer data platform that synchronizes and activates user data for segmentation and omnichannel messaging.
- [Analytics](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/analytics/): campaign and per-message stats, conversion funnels, D1/D7/D30 retention, RFM grid, custom dashboards, event streaming, data export.
- [Predictive Marketing Analytics](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/predictive-marketing-analytics/): ML scoring for churn (85% precision, 30 days ahead), conversion, and LTV — no data science team required.
- [AI-Powered Personalization](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/ai-powered-personalization/): purchase-intent scoring, churn prediction 72 hours ahead, autonomous segmentation, dynamic content across all channels.
- [ManyMoneyAI Marketing Copilot](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/ai-marketer/): autonomous AI that detects underperforming campaigns, finds high-intent customers, launches and optimizes campaigns; included in every plan, activates in ~30 minutes.
- [Omnichannel Personalization](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/personalization/): AI-built segments from plain-language descriptions, Liquid templates, Connected Content pulling live backend data.
- [A/B Testing](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/marketing-ab-testing/): variant testing across push, email, in-app, and SMS with automatic statistical significance and multi-armed bandit optimization.
- [Multi-Channel Orchestration](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/multi-channel-orchestration/): cross-channel journeys with fallback logic, frequency capping, and AI channel selection.
- [Event-Triggered Marketing](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/event-triggered-marketing/): any tracked event launches multi-channel campaigns in milliseconds; 3–5x higher conversion vs scheduled sends.

## Solutions by industry

- [E-commerce](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/e-commerce-solution/): cart abandonment recovery, behavioral segmentation, and lifecycle messaging; case studies report +70% sales from cart recovery and +40% AOV from personalization.
- [Gaming](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/gaming/): player engagement and monetization — event-based segmentation, LiveOps messaging, recurring deals; clients include G5 Games, Ankama, Peoplefun.
- [Mobile Games (retention focus)](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-for-mobile-games/): behavioral triggers, tournament Live Activities, win-back automation; justDice cut churn 26% across 20+ apps.
- [Fintech & Banking](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/fintech-banking/): secure transactional and marketing messaging with SOC 2/ISO 27001/GDPR compliance; AvaTrade converted 12% of anonymous users to registered accounts.
- [Neo-banks & Digital Wallets](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-for-finance-apps/): API-first delivery, 99.9% transactional delivery rate, 10M+ banking alerts daily, Live Activities for balances and transfers.
- [Trading Platforms](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-for-trading-apps/): real-time trade alerts (15M+ daily), portfolio-personalized signals, API triggers from trading engines.
- [Telecom](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/telecom/): subscriber lifecycle messaging; reported results: −25% churn, +18% ARPU, +45% self-service app engagement.
- [News & Media](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/media/): high-speed delivery, iOS Live Activities, CMS/API content flows; GB News sends 12M daily pushes with 72.2% opt-in; EU (Germany) data center.
- [Mobility](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/mobility/): ride status on the lock screen via iOS Live Activities and Android Live Updates, Time-Sensitive driver arrival alerts, push-to-SMS/WhatsApp fallback via reachability check, rider and driver apps in one account.
- [Food Delivery](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/delivery/): live order status via iOS Live Activities and Android Live Updates, order-event journeys, Time-Sensitive courier alerts, push-to-SMS/WhatsApp fallback, RFM segments by order history, wallet loyalty cards.
- [Delivery Apps & Quick Commerce](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-for-delivery-apps/): reorder automation, geo-triggered alerts, AI campaigns; case: +47% campaign revenue in 90 days.
- [Subscription Apps](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/subscription-based-apps/): conversion-path tracking and paywall nudges; reported up to 67% conversion to subscription and +34% MRR.
- [EdTech & Learning Apps](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-for-e-learning/): streak reminders, onboarding journeys, assignment Live Activities; 3x higher course completion with streak campaigns.

## Use cases

- [Cart Abandonment Recovery](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/cart-abandonment-recovery/): automated reminders and incentives across push, email, and in-app.
- [Increase User Retention](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/increase-user-retention/): AI churn prediction 72 hours ahead plus lifecycle campaigns from onboarding to win-back.
- [Churn Prevention Campaigns](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/churn-prevention-campaigns/): early disengagement detection and automated retention offers; 35% fewer cancellations in case data.
- [Reduce Churn Rate](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/reduce-churn-rate/): predictive churn management for subscription products with risk thresholds and dunning sequences.
- [Win Back Dormant Users](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/win-back-dormant-users/): reactivation campaigns; case: 16% dormant-user reactivation, 2.6x MAU.
- [Customer Onboarding Journeys](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-onboarding-journey/): multi-channel onboarding; 2x Day-1 activation, 75% completion in case data.
- [First Purchase Onboarding](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/first-purchase-onboarding/): purchase-triggered welcome flows that drive repeat purchases.
- [Post-Purchase Communication](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/post-purchase-communication/): order confirmations, shipping updates, review requests, cross-sell with live order data.
- [Boost App Engagement](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/boost-app-engagement/): behavioral triggers that grow DAU and feature adoption (case: DAU 15%→28% in 60 days).
- [Drive Revenue Growth](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/drive-revenue-growth/): AI campaign optimization targeting ARPU, LTV, and conversions; case: +43% quarterly revenue.
- [Player Re-engagement](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/player-reengagement/): win-back for lapsed players with at-risk scoring and channel escalation.
- [Player Monetization Journeys](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/player-monetization-journey/): spending-tier segmentation (non-spenders to whales) with triggers on in-game events.
- [VIP / Whale Management](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/vip-player-management/): retention automation for top spenders who drive ~70% of mobile game revenue.
- [In-Game Events Promotion](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/in-game-events-promotion/): countdown sequences and behavioral targeting for LiveOps events.
- [Smart Coupon Journeys](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/smart-coupons-journey/): behavior-triggered coupon campaigns with margin-protecting discount logic.
- [Replenishment Reminders](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/replenishment-reminders/): reorder reminders timed to product lifecycle.
- [Birthday & Anniversary Campaigns](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/birthday-anniversary-campaigns/): automated milestone sequences; typical results 52% open rate, 22% conversion.
- [Plan Upgrade Campaigns](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/plan-upgrade-campaigns/): usage-milestone triggers and in-app prompts for subscription upgrades.
- [Telecom: Bill Payment Reminders](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/bill-payment-reminders/): multi-touch dunning with one-tap payment links (+40% on-time payments).
- [Telecom: Roaming Notifications](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/roaming-notifications/): border-crossing alerts and roaming package promotion.
- [Telecom: Data Usage Alerts](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/data-usage-alerts/): real-time threshold alerts preventing bill shock.
- [Telecom: Network Outage Communications](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/network-outage-communications/): API-triggered, geo-targeted incident alerts with SMS failsafe (−65% support calls during outages).
- [Healthcare: Seasonal Campaigns](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/seasonal-health-marketing/): HIPAA-compliant patient reminders (flu shots, screenings, wellness visits).
- [For Marketing Teams](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/marketing-team-solution/): no-code campaign and journey building with approval workflows and role-based permissions.
- [For Product Managers](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/product-manager-solution/): in-app onboarding tours, checklists, and feature-discovery tooltips for product-led growth.

## Compare Pushwoosh

- [Pushwoosh vs Braze](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-vs-braze/): device-based pricing from $0 vs data-point billing (Braze typically $60K–100K+/yr); 2–10 day integration vs 6+ week onboarding; no minimum spend.
- [Pushwoosh vs OneSignal](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-vs-onesignal/): unlimited journeys (OneSignal caps at 3–20), full RFM and event-based segmentation, 1-year+ data retention (OneSignal deletes API/Journeys data after 30 days), WhatsApp and wallet passes included.
- [Pushwoosh vs Firebase (FCM)](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-vs-firebase/): full marketing automation layer — 6 channels, visual journey builder, segmentation, analytics — on top of what FCM only delivers.
- [Pushwoosh vs CleverTap](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-vs-clevertap/): no feature gating across plans, free onboarding, AI copilot included on every plan.
- [Pushwoosh vs MoEngage](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-vs-moengage/): device-based vs MTU pricing, live trigger editing, private US/Germany data servers, ~1-month full rollout.
- [Pushwoosh vs Customer.io](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/pushwoosh-vs-customer-io/): mobile-first vs email-centric; no-code Dynamic Content, RFM segmentation, and live campaign editing without per-contact overages.

## Integrations

Full catalog: https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/

- [Segment](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/segment/): streams events and audiences into Pushwoosh in real time.
- [mParticle](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/mparticle/): syncs audiences, events, and user data for behavior-triggered messaging.
- [Solitics](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/solitics/): real-time customer data sync for personalized journeys.
- [Amplitude](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/amplitude/): syncs events and cohorts for behavioral triggers and segmentation.
- [Mixpanel](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/mixpanel/): imports cohorts and behavioral data for targeted campaigns.
- [Google Analytics](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/google-analytics/): exports GA behavior segments into Pushwoosh for targeting.
- [Piano Analytics](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/piano/): two-way sync — Piano segments in, engagement stats back.
- [Firebase Crashlytics](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/crashlytics/): targets users affected by specific crashes with notifications.
- [AppsFlyer](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/appsflyer/): attribution and in-app event data for personalized journeys.
- [AppsFlyer ESP 2.0](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/appsflyer-esp2/): email click attribution preserving Universal Links deep linking.
- [Adjust](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/adjust/): in-app event sync for data-driven engagement campaigns.
- [Singular](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/singular/): two-way attribution sync including push-driven app opens.
- [RevenueCat](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/revenuecat/): subscription events for renewal, upsell, and payment-recovery flows.
- [Adapty](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/adapty/): subscription and paywall events for upsell and renewal campaigns.
- [Qonversion](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/qonversion/): subscription, purchase, and attribution data for retention automation.
- [Stripe](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/stripe/): payment and subscription events for revenue attribution and segmentation.
- [Shopify](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/shopify/): customers and orders sync for cart recovery and order updates.
- [Magento](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/magento/): Magento 2 customers, orders, and abandoned carts for recovery campaigns.
- [Meta Ads](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/meta-ads/): syncs Pushwoosh segments into Meta Custom Audiences for retargeting and suppression.
- [HubSpot](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/hubspot/): CRM contact and activity sync for omnichannel campaigns.
- [Marketo](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/marketo/): triggers web push from Marketo landing page and lead behavior.
- [Event Streaming](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/event-streaming/): streams Pushwoosh user events to external systems via HTTP or gRPC.
- [Inbound Webhook](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/inbound-webhook/): any third-party tool can trigger customer journeys, no server required.
- [WebViewGold](https://www.pushwoosh.com/integrations/webviewgold/): adds push, in-app, and email to WebViewGold-wrapped apps without coding.

## For developers

- [Pushwoosh API](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/api/): REST API for push, email, SMS, WhatsApp, iOS Live Activities, segmentation, events, webhooks — full feature parity with the dashboard.
- [Gaming API Platform](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/gaming-api-platform/): API-first stack for game studios; Unity/Unreal integration in 2–4 hours, 500K API calls/sec, OpenAPI specs and Postman collections.
- [Messaging MCP](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/mcp/): hosted MCP server (beta) — one Notify tool lets AI agents send to 8 channels (push, email, SMS, WhatsApp, Telegram, LINE, Kakao); scoped tokens, idempotent sends.
- [ManyMoney MCP](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/manymoney-mcp/): Notify and NotifyBulk tools for AI agents; works with Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf; free up to 1,000 MAU.
- [Developer Documentation](https://docs.pushwoosh.com): SDK guides, API reference, integration tutorials.
- [GitHub](https://github.com/Pushwoosh/): open-source SDKs and sample apps.

## Trust and company

- [Why Pushwoosh](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/why-pushwoosh/): 14+ years in messaging; minimal data collection with full client control over data access.
- [Data Safety](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/data-safety/): ISO 27001:2022 certified, SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA; privately owned enterprise-grade infrastructure, 24/7 availability monitoring.
- [Enterprise Solution](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/enterprise-solution/): SSO/SAML/RBAC, private cloud or dedicated infrastructure, 100M+ users per org, P1 support response under 15 minutes.
- [Customer Testimonials](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/testimonials/): reviews and case metrics — up to 91.9% push CTR, +37% D30 retention, 5–25M notifications daily per client.
- [Pricing](https://www.pushwoosh.com/pricing/): transparent pay-as-you-go calculator; free up to 1,000 MAU.
- [Book a Demo](https://www.pushwoosh.com/demo/): guided product walkthrough with the team.

## Optional

- [Blog](https://www.pushwoosh.com/blog/): best practices, benchmarks (e.g. push notification CTR by industry), case studies, product updates.
- [All Products](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/): full catalog of channels, capabilities, and solutions.
- [eBooks](https://www.pushwoosh.com/ebooks/): research reports and guides, including push notification benchmark studies.
- [Webinars](https://www.pushwoosh.com/webinars/): recorded product and strategy sessions.
- [Sitemap](https://www.pushwoosh.com/sitemap-index.xml): full URL inventory including all 14 language versions.

# Products

---

## A/B/n split testing inside the customer journey

URL: https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/abn-split/

Split journey traffic across up to 4 branches, score each one against your conversion goals, and route new users to the winning branch automatically once the result is significant.

Keywords: A/B/n split testing, in-journey A/B testing, journey split testing, customer journey A/B test, automatic winner selection, conversion goal testing, split traffic allocation

A/B/n split testing

### Find the **winning variant** inside your journey

Split journey traffic across up to 4 branches, each with its own copy, timing, or channel. Pushwoosh scores every branch against your conversion goals and sends new users down the one that performs best.

Book a demo

Start for free

## Everything you need to run a split test

**Up to 4 branches**

Branch A is the control. You set the traffic share for each branch.

**Random allocation**

Every new entrant is assigned by the percentages you configure.

**Goal-driven results**

Track 1 conversion event or several, each scored separately.

**Significance built in**

Z-Score and P-Value, marked Significant at 90% confidence.

**Automatic winner routing**

New users are routed to the winning branch without a manual step.

**In-flight users protected**

Anyone already in a branch finishes the path they started.

## What each branch can change

Drop the A/B/n Split element anywhere on the journey canvas and give it 2 to 4 branches. Each branch runs its own sub-flow, so a variant can differ by message copy, by delay length, by channel, or by sending nothing at all. Traffic percentages have to add up to 100%, and a reset control puts them back to an even distribution.

- **Branch A** – the control, either the flow you run today or a fresh baseline.
- **Branches B, C and D** – the challengers, each with its own messages, delays and channels.
- **Traffic share** – any split that totals 100%. An even split reaches significance fastest.

The split element carries no messaging logic of its own. It decides who goes where, and the channel blocks underneath it do the sending.

## Two ways to close a test

### Automatic winner selection

The platform watches your goal continuously. Once a branch clears the 90% confidence bar, Pushwoosh deactivates the underperforming branches and sends every new entrant to the winner.

That happens whether or not anyone is looking at the dashboard.

### Manual control when you want it

Manual mode surfaces the same live statistics and leaves the call to you. Read the numbers, then click **Keep only winner** to deactivate the losing branches.

The journey keeps running while you decide. Closing a test does not require pausing it.

**Deactivation applies to new entrants only.** Users already assigned to a branch complete the path they were given, whatever happens to that branch afterwards.

## What A/B/n split testing is best for

**Cart abandonment**

Test reminder copy and delay length, then keep the version that recovers more carts.

**Paywall and trial messages**

A/B the wording or the timing of a trial-ending message against your conversion event.

**Digest headlines and send times**

Run 2 headlines or 2 send times on a recurring digest and score them on opens or clicks.

**Channel preference**

Send the same message on push, email and SMS to find out which one converts for a segment.

**Monetization offers in games**

Test offer copy or timing inside a re-engagement journey, with purchase events as the goal.

**Win-back timing**

Compare how long to wait before reaching out to a dormant user.

### One journey, every channel

The split element sits on the same canvas as every channel block, so a branch can carry mobile push, in-app messages, email, SMS, WhatsApp or web push against a single customer profile.

You build the test where the journey already runs, inside the [Customer Journey Builder](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/), instead of wiring up a separate experimentation tool alongside it.

## Three ways to design the test

**Current flow vs a new idea**

Branch A keeps what you send today. B, C and D carry the challengers.

**New idea vs new idea**

No incumbent involved. Pick one new version as the control and score the rest against it.

**Message vs no message**

Give one branch an equal Time Delay and no message, to measure whether the touch moves the metric at all.

### How a winner is decided

Define at least 1 conversion goal before the test can launch. A goal is a tracked event you already send to Pushwoosh: a purchase, a checkout, a subscription start, a level completion.

Pushwoosh scores each branch against the control with a Z-Score and a P-Value, and marks the result Significant at a 90% confidence level.

Several goals can run on the same test at once. Results are calculated separately per goal, and you choose which goal to read when more than one is live.

## Testing on infrastructure you can name

Pushwoosh runs on its own hardware in the US and Germany, under GDPR and BDSG. Your test data, goal events and customer profiles stay on the same platform that sends the messages.

Full certification detail on the data safety page.

## How it works

**Pause the journey and add the split**

## What it does

A segment is a tree of conditions, tags, events, geo, platform, even other segments, joined with AND, OR, or exclude. ## The format, **in full**

Every Android notification belongs to a channel, a user-controlled category such as "Promotions", "Order updates" or "Breaking news". The channel is what lets someone mute one type of message without blocking the app that sends it.

**Named channel, created server-side**

Add `pw_channel` to Android root params in the Control Panel, or to `android_root_params` in `/createMessage`. The first push naming a new channel creates it on the device, with no app release needed.

**Default channel, out of the box**

The SDK creates a default channel on every Android 8+ device automatically, even when `pw_channel` is left empty, so a notification always has somewhere valid to land.

**Importance level**

The Importance level field (`-2` to `2`) sets how the channel behaves on arrival, from silent to a full heads-up banner. It is read once, at the moment the channel is created.

**Custom sound per channel**

Pair `pw_channel` with `android_sound`, a file placed in `res/raw`, and every push into that channel plays its own sound instead of the system default.

### What you control

| What you send | What it does | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A channel name | Creates the channel on first send, or reuses the one already on the device | `pw_channel` in Android root params, or the API payload |
| An Importance level, `-2` to `2` | Sets heads-up behavior, fixed the moment the channel is created | The Importance level field on the push, or the same value via the API |
| `android_sound` + `pw_channel` | Gives that one channel its own alert sound | A file in `res/raw`, referenced by name without an extension |
| No `pw_channel` sent | The SDK creates and uses a default channel automatically | No setup, out of the box on Android 8+ |

### Where you set it

**One field in the composer**

Type a channel name into Android root params in the Send-Push form or a preset. A new category needs no release and no developer.

**One key in the API**

`android_root_params.pw_channel` in `/createMessage`, alongside `android_sound` for a channel-specific alert sound.

**The same logic on every Android transport**

The identical `pw_channel` payload works over FCM, and over Huawei HMS and Amazon ADM through [Alt-store push](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/alt-store-push/).

## The job it does, **inside a journey**

### The same Journey runs **two channels**

The channel is an attribute of the push you are already sending, so it needs no separate integration to wire up. A transactional branch names one channel, a promotional branch names another, and both run from the same audience and the same [Customer Journey](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/) as the rest of your [mobile push](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/mobile-push-notifications/).

### The order alert rings while the sale stays quiet

An order-placed event fires the Journey. A silent push quietly prefetches the delivery estimate in the background, and the transactional branch names the "Order updates" channel with a high Importance level, so it posts as a heads-up alert.

The same Journey runs a separate branch into a "Promotions" channel at default importance. A user who mutes Promotions keeps getting order alerts on the same phone: the two run as separate channels inside one app.

## What to use it for

Channels pay off in proportion to how many genuinely different types of notification an app sends. One uniform stream gets almost nothing from them; a mix of loud promotions and quiet transactional alerts gets the most.

| Industry | Channels worth separating | Why it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mobile games | Events & promotions vs guild & social vs rewards vs live-ops alerts | High stream diversity on an Android-heavy install base |
| Creator & subscription apps | New content vs social interactions vs billing vs promotions | Subscribers get what they signed up for, and nothing else |
| E-commerce & retail | Promotions vs order & delivery updates vs price-drop alerts | The classic promo-versus-transactional split |
| Marketplaces | Buyer/seller messages vs order updates vs promotions vs listing alerts | Multi-sided messaging is naturally multi-stream |
| Fintech & banking | Fraud & transaction alerts vs statements vs reminders vs promotions | Must-deliver alerts sit next to fully optional promotions |
| Media, news & streaming | Breaking news vs topic feeds vs new episodes vs promotions | The textbook Android channel use case |

### When it isn't worth the setup

- Reaching someone new: the channel only sorts a message the push already sent.
- Anything on iOS: channels do nothing there, and [Time-Sensitive or Critical levels](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/time-sensitive-critical-levels/) handle the same job.
- Making a heads-up alert retroactive: importance is fixed the moment a channel is created, and a new behavior needs a new channel name.
- A long list of near-duplicate channels: it reads as clutter and trains users to mute the whole group.
- An app with one real stream of notifications: there is nothing to separate, so a channel adds a setting nobody needs.

The channel decides where it lands. The words decide if it gets read

## Platform & technical coverage

Notification channels are an Android-only OS primitive, introduced in Android 8.0 Oreo. iOS has no channel to register; the comparable job runs through [Time-Sensitive and Critical interruption levels](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/time-sensitive-critical-levels/) instead, and the web has no equivalent either. The last column says where Pushwoosh's mechanic ends and the operating system's rules begin.

| Capability | iOS | Android | Web | Delivered by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Notification channels | – | Android 8.0 Oreo (API 26) and later | – | Native OS primitive, Pushwoosh SDK 5.4.0+ |
| Default channel | – | Yes, created automatically | – | The Pushwoosh SDK, on every Android 8+ device |
| Named channel via `pw_channel` | – | Yes, created on first send, no app release | – | Android root params field, or `/createMessage` |
| Custom sound per channel | – | Yes | – | `pw_channel` + `android_sound`, a file in `res/raw` |
| Same mechanic on Huawei & Amazon devices | – | Yes, via HMS and ADM | – | [Alt-store push](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/alt-store-push/) |
| Cross-platform SDK wrappers | – | Cordova/Capacitor, React Native, Unity, Flutter | – | Routed through the native Android bridge |
| Runtime permission required first | – | Android 13+, `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` | – | The OS, before any channel can show |
| The comparable urgency control | [Time-Sensitive / Critical levels](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/time-sensitive-critical-levels/) | Channel importance, set here | – | A separate feature per platform |

## How it works

**Compose _(no-code)_**

Type a channel name into Android root params in the Send-Push form, or send `android_root_params.pw_channel` through the [Messages API](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/api/).

**Set it up once**

The first push naming a new channel creates it on the device with the importance, sound and vibration from that message. Plan a taxonomy of 3 to 5 channels up front, since changing the behavior later needs a new channel name.

**Orchestrate _(no-code)_**

Route each channel from the matching branch of the same [Customer Journey](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/), using the same audience and profile as the rest of your messaging.

## Limits worth knowing

**A categorization primitive with strict Android rules. These are its edges.**

- Android only. Channels do nothing on iOS, and [Time-Sensitive and Critical levels](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/time-sensitive-critical-levels/) handle the same job there.
- Importance, sound and vibration lock in the moment a channel is created. A later push into the same channel cannot change them, so a new behavior needs a new channel name.
- The user has the final say. Anyone can mute or fully block a channel in system settings, and that decision cannot be reversed from the server.
- Android 13 and later require the `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` runtime permission before any channel can show at all.
- Android 14 surfaces a channel's importance to the user, and Android 15 auto-cools rapid repeat notifications, so a miscategorized channel gets muted fast.
- The channel name is a free-text key. A typo creates a new, unintended channel instead of reusing the one you meant.
- Server-side visibility into channel usage is a floor rather than a coverage metric. The default channel leaves no marker in the payload, so we don't report what share of senders use named channels.

## The format, **in full**

A badge is a single integer, and that is the whole appeal. It costs no banner and no sound, it spends none of the permission you fought to get, and it keeps working on the user who swiped your push away three hours ago. There are three things you can do to that integer from the composer or the API, plus one caveat about where it actually renders.

**An exact count**

`ios_badges: 5` puts a 5 on the icon, whatever was there before. The value you send is the value the user sees, which is what you want when your server already knows the real total.

**`+1` and `-1`**

Relative changes bump or drop the count without you tracking it. The SDK posts the on-device value back through the internal `/setBadge` endpoint, so Pushwoosh's counter stays level with the real icon.

**`0` clears it**

Send `0` and the badge leaves the icon. Clearing on open is the difference between a count users trust and a red dot they learn to ignore.

**iOS uniform, **Android launcher-dependent****

On iOS the badge is a standard `aps.badge` value and every device draws it identically. On Android there is no native badge API, so the render depends on the launcher, and Pushwoosh says so rather than implying coverage it cannot deliver.

### What you control

| What you send | What happens to the count | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An integer, `5` | Sets the badge to exactly that value | `ios_badges` / `android_badges`, or the Badges field |
| `+1`, `+3` | Increments the current count | Same field. Also `+n` in the Android presets |
| `-1` | Decrements the current count | Same field, for a read or a dismissal on the server side |
| `0` | Removes the badge from the icon | Same field, or the app on launch |
| An SDK call | Sets or clears the badge from an in-app event | `setApplicationIconBadgeNumber` on iOS, `PushwooshBadge` on Android |
| Nothing | The SDK applies whatever badge arrived with the push | No app code for the basic iOS case |
| An extension | Changes the count before the notification is displayed | `PWNotificationExtensionManager` with App Groups |

### Where you set it

**A Badges field in the composer**

The Send-Push form and the push presets take a number, `+n`, `-n` or `0`. Changing what a campaign does to the count takes no release and no developer.

**One key in the API**

`ios_badges` and `android_badges` in `/createMessage`. On iOS the value is rendered into the `aps.badge` field of the payload Apple already carries.

**Applied and synced by the SDK**

The SDK applies the arriving value with no app code, and keeps the server's notion of the badge current through `/setBadge` so `+1` counts from the right number.

## The job it does, **inside a journey**

### One count, **several sources**

The badge is an attribute of a message you are already sending, so it needs no integration of its own. The same [Customer Journey](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/) and the same customer profile that decide who gets the push also decide what the count becomes.

So the only open question is what feeds the number. A [Message Inbox](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/message-inbox/) unread total can be the count outright, a silent push can move it with no alert at all, and a visible [mobile push](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/mobile-push-notifications/) carries it along for the ride. A step at the journey goal takes it back to `0`.

### Three rewards stack up while the player is away

Each reward granted fires an event, and each event sends a silent push that adds `+1`. Nothing rings, nothing lights up the lock screen, and by the evening the icon quietly reads 3.

When the live event opens, the same Journey sends one visible push worth interrupting for. Whichever of the two brings the player back, the SDK clears the badge to `0` on launch, so tomorrow's count starts from something true.

## What to use it for

The badge pays off in proportion to count-density: whether your app has a real, building number of unread or pending things worth putting on an icon. Apps built around a counter get a genuine re-engagement nudge for free, and apps with nothing to count get a red dot that trains users to ignore red dots.

| Moment | What the number means | Why the badge fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mobile games · rewards, refilled lives, event entries | 3 things to collect | The count is part of the retention loop already, and collecting is the whole motivation |
| Creator & subscription apps · drops, DMs, comments | 12 unread | A social feed keeps this number internally, so the icon only has to show it |
| Media & news · unread stories, new episodes | 5 unread stories | The textbook case, and the one that reliably brings a reader back into a session |
| E-commerce & marketplaces · cart items, unread offers | 2 items in your cart | A quiet reminder that costs the shopper none of their attention to receive |
| Fintech · statements, alerts, pending actions | 1 action needed | There is a real unread-document count, and the icon carries it without putting detail on a lock screen |
| Trading & betting · triggered alerts, settled bets | 4 alerts fired | Alerts pile up into a number that actually means something to the user |
| Healthcare & telemed · results, secure messages | Your results are in | The count travels on the home screen while the content stays behind authentication |
| EdTech · unread lessons, streaks, assignments | 2 lessons waiting | A streak or a lesson queue is exactly the kind of number people close out |

### When the badge is the wrong tool

The badge reports a quantity. Everything about what is waiting, and how urgently, belongs to another surface.

- The user needs to know what arrived: that is a [mobile push](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/mobile-push-notifications/), a rich media push or an [in-app message](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/in-app-messaging/).
- The moment cannot wait. A badge is passive by design, so urgency belongs to an [interruption level](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/time-sensitive-critical-levels/).
- The state is ongoing rather than counted: an order en route, a running score. That is a [Live Activity](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/live-updates/).
- The app has no natural building count. Insurance, hotels, utilities and single-session tools get one bill or one booking, and a badge there is noise.
- Your audience is Android-heavy and the badge would be a primary mechanic. Treat it as best-effort there and design the flow to work without it.

The count gets them looking. The push still has to be worth opening

## Platform & technical coverage

iOS has one badge, and every iPhone draws it the same way. Android has no universal badge API, so what appears on the home screen is up to the launcher the user happens to be running. The last column names whatever actually draws the number, because for this feature that is where the honest answer lives.

| Update the badge with no alert | Yes | Best-effort | – | A silent push, same audience and Journey |

## Security & hosting

Pushwoosh runs on its own hardware in the US and Germany, under GDPR and BDSG.

## How it works

Setting a badge is no-code and free on every plan. The engineering time sits in two narrow places, and neither of them is the iOS basic case.

**Compose the count _(no-code)_**

Type a number, `+n`, `-n` or `0` in the **Badges** field of the Send-Push form or a preset, or send `ios_badges` and `android_badges` through the [Messages API](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/api/). On iOS the basic case needs nothing from your app: the SDK applies the value on arrival.

**Wire the two places that need it _(developer)_**

Android needs the `com.pushwoosh:pushwoosh-badge` library plus the launcher-specific permissions in the manifest. Clearing on push-open and app-launch is one SDK call, and a Notification Service Extension with App Groups is only for counts that have to change before display.

**Orchestrate it _(no-code)_**

Drive the number from your [Message Inbox](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/message-inbox/) unread total, move it with a silent push that shows no alert, and clear it at the goal of the same [Customer Journey](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/) that runs your push, in-app and email.

Read the Messages API reference

## Limits worth knowing

**A count primitive with one uniform platform and one fragmented one. These are its edges.**

- iOS is uniform and first-class. Android is best-effort, because the OS has no universal badge API and the launcher decides what appears.
- Android coverage is genuinely uneven. Samsung and Xiaomi use different mechanisms, Google's own Pixel launcher largely does not render icon badges, and some third-party launchers ignore them.
- Android badge updates are battery-gated. Doze and App Standby throttle the background work they depend on, and a force-stopped app cannot update the count until it is reopened.
- Huawei devices hand badge control to Huawei's own launcher, so behavior varies by device and EMUI or HarmonyOS version.
- Relative `+1` and `-1` depend on the SDK knowing the current value. An app that overrides the badge without syncing can leave a server-side increment counting from the wrong number, and iOS offers no API to read the system badge back.
- Badge-via-push mechanics changed in iOS SDK **6.4.0**. Apps that used the badge to count received pushes had to migrate, so plan against the current behavior rather than the legacy one.
- The badge carries a quantity and nothing else. What is waiting, and how urgent it is, has to come from a push, an in-app message or an interruption level.
- It leaves almost no server-side marker. Only campaigns that explicitly set the badge appear in the stored payload, while SDK-managed apply and clear do not, so measure it by running a badged cohort against an unbadged one rather than looking for it in a report.

Customer Journey Builder

### Best time to send

Best time to send calculates a personal delivery window for each push or email step, based on that person's own history of opens, and falls back to a time you set when there isn't enough history yet.

Book a demo

Start for free

## The same minute, a hundred different mornings

A journey fires a push the moment its trigger condition is met, at one server minute, for everyone who qualifies. Some of those people are mid-commute and glance at the phone right away. Some are asleep. Some put the phone down after breakfast and won't pick it up again until lunch. None of that shows up in the send report: the count goes up the same whether the message landed in someone's hand or their notification shade at 6am. Best time to send is what turns "the trigger fired" into "it arrived when this specific person was actually likely to look."

## What it calculates, and what it falls back to

At each push or email step with Best time to send turned on, Pushwoosh looks at the last 30 days of that person's own history: `PW_ApplicationOpen` and `PW_NotificationOpen` for push, `PW_EmailOpen` for email. It finds the hour they open most often and delivers within the next 24 hours of entering the step. The more of that history exists, the more the calculated hour can be trusted. Someone with barely any opens on file gets the Default time you set instead, delivered in their own local time.

| Setting | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Channels | Push and email steps inside Customer Journey Builder | — |
| History lookback | Last 30 days of that person's opens, recalculated every time they enter the step | 30 days |
| Delivery horizon | The calculated hour always falls within the next 24 hours of entry | 24 hours |
| Data source | PW_ApplicationOpen + PW_NotificationOpen (push), PW_EmailOpen (email) | — |
| Fallback | Default time you set, delivered in the recipient's own local time, used when history is too thin | Marketer-set Default time |

It's a personal calculation from that recipient's own opens, recalculated at every entry, rather than one best hour applied to the whole segment.

### Recalculated on every journey entry

Pushwoosh works this out fresh each time someone reaches the step, from the last 30 days of history available at that exact moment. That's what keeps the estimate current: a subscriber who only recently started opening pushes regularly gets a better-informed hour than they would have last week, without anyone touching the setting.

## Why Customer Journey Builder needs this

A journey that runs unattended sends whenever its logic fires, whether or not anyone's actually looking at their phone right then. [Customer Journey Builder](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/) can sequence a launch, a renewal reminder, or a daily reminder without anyone watching the clock, but only if something inside it accounts for the fact that "now" means something different for every recipient. Best time to send is what lets a journey stay automated and still land inside the window each person is actually likely to check.

## How it works

**Turn on the standard events first**

Enable PW_ApplicationOpen and PW_NotificationOpen for push, or PW_EmailOpen for email, a few days before you send, so there's real history to calculate against.

**Turn on Best time to send on the step**

Open the push or email step's settings, flip the toggle, and set a Default time for the fallback — it's delivered in each recipient's own local time automatically.

**Check how often the fallback fires**

A high share of sends going out at Default time usually means the audience doesn't have much open history yet.

Read the docs

## One control among several that decide when a message lands

Best time to send decides the hour, inside a 24-hour window, that a push or email goes out. [Reachability check](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/reachability-check/) decides which channel it goes out on, routing around one that's closed. A [Time Delay](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/time-delay/) set to a specific date and time still runs on its own clock: if that exact moment falls before the send time Best time to send calculated for that person, the send never goes out and the person exits the journey, with nothing in the reports to flag why. Combine the two, and check which one is meant to win before you rely on a specific order.

### A Time Delay set to an exact date can still cut in front

## Match the message to what you actually know

You want to message people who've spent over $50 differently from everyone who opened the app once and left. That's one condition, easy to hold in your head. It gets harder the week marketing wants trial users on app version 2.1 who haven't cleared level 12, three separate facts about one person, and a segment can only use what's already recorded against them.

A tag is where that fact lives before any journey or campaign can act on it.

## What a tag can hold

A tag attaches one piece of data to a device or to a user, in one of 7 types.

| Type | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| String | Text, like an email, a subscription tier, or a name |
| Integer | Whole numbers, like a level reached or loyalty points |
| List | Several values on one tag at once, like favorite categories or interests |
| Boolean | True or false, like opted into a program or finished onboarding |
| Date | A calendar date, stored as a Unix timestamp |
| Price | A currency-formatted value, in ISO 4217 format |
| Version | An app version number, compared the way version numbers should be |

Every tag also carries a scope. General stores the value per device, so two phones under the same person can hold different values. User-specific stores it per user ID instead, and one update applies across every device that person owns.

Price compares as currency and Version compares as a version number. Most tag systems leave both as plain strings for you to parse.

Some tags need no setup at all: Language, Country, App version, and Last Application Open arrive with the SDK, ready to segment on from day one.

### Pick a type and a scope when you create it

Custom tags are named and typed once, in the Control Panel or through the API. General scope covers per-device facts like a cart total; User-specific scope covers facts that belong to the person, like a loyalty tier or lifetime spend.

## The data every segment and message reads

[Actionable CDP](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/cdp/) exists to turn stored data into messaging decisions: a segment that fires, a branch that routes, a placeholder that fills in with the right name. A tag is the fact it reads to make that call. Default tags cover what the SDK already collects; a custom tag covers the one attribute your business actually runs on, like lifetime spend or subscription tier.

## How the 3 condition types differ

Every Condition split element checks exactly one type of condition against the user's current profile, then sends them down the matching branch. The check runs once, the moment the user reaches the element.

| Condition type | Branches | What it checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Segment | Exactly 2 | Whether the user currently belongs to a segment you pick: Users in a segment, or All other users |
| Tag | 1 to 10, by operator | The current value of a tag on the profile, one branch per value you define |
| Event attribute | 1 to 10, by operator | The value of an attribute on an event that already fired earlier in the journey |

The branch ceiling for Tag and Event attribute depends on the operator behind each branch. Value-matching operators such as equals, in, or contains reach the full 10. Comparison operators such as not-equal, greater-or-equal, or exists cap lower, since a branch built on one of those already covers most of the range on its own.

A journey can't mix condition types inside one element, and a segment, tag, or event has to already exist in the account. The element itself doesn't create any of them. It sits inside [Customer Journey Builder](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/), reading the same segments, tags, and events the rest of the canvas already uses.

### Every configuration keeps a way out

Configure Segment, Tag, or Event attribute, and All other users ships with every version of the element by default. There's no toggle for it, and no way to delete it.

A user whose tag value matches none of the branches you built still lands somewhere, on a path you control instead of leaving the journey.

### Stack elements for a condition on top of a condition

One element reads one condition type. For "Premium subscriber and high spend", place a Condition split with a Segment condition for Premium first, then add a second Condition split with a Tag condition for spend level on the branch that already matched Premium.

Each element stays simple to read on the canvas, and the chain carries the compound logic that one crowded rule would otherwise hold.

## FAQ

Q: What's the difference between Condition split and Wait for Trigger?

A: Condition split checks data already on the profile the moment the user arrives, with no wait. Wait for Trigger pauses and watches for a new event to fire within a window. [See Wait for Trigger](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/wait-for-trigger/).

Q: Can I combine a segment condition and a tag condition in one element?

A: No. Each element reads one condition type. Chain a second Condition split on the branch that already matched the first condition to combine them.

Q: Why does Segment only give me 2 branches?

A: Segment membership is binary: a user is either in the segment or not. For more than 2 branches, split on a Tag or an Event attribute instead.

Q: What happens to a user who doesn't match any branch I configured?

A: They land on All other users, a branch every Condition split element carries by default and that can't be removed.

Q: Can this element create a tag or segment that doesn't exist yet?

A: No. The segment, tag, or event has to already exist in the account before Condition split can route on it.

## Nobody checks the order of events until an audit does

An unsubscribe link fixes the wrong problem. GDPR and CCPA ask for more than "stop messaging someone who opted out." They ask for proof that data collection itself never started before consent did. That's a sequencing question, and most consent handling on the market answers it after the fact, with tags bolted onto data already collected. Consent management holds the collection itself dormant until a user says yes, and puts it back to sleep the moment they say no.

## Two mechanisms, one gate

| Mechanism | Platforms | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SDK gateway | iOS, Android, Unity, Web | Holds data collection off from launch until you turn it on, and off again if consent is withdrawn |
| double opt-in toggle | Subscription forms | One project-wide toggle: new signups get a confirmation email with a 24-hour link before they're added |

The SDK gateway starts dormant through configuration set before launch: an Info.plist key on iOS, a manifest flag on Android and Unity, an init parameter on Web. Once consent arrives, the platform's own enable call takes over, and the same call in reverse turns collection back off if someone withdraws consent. The exact name differs per platform; the shape doesn't.

The double opt-in toggle is the part most competitors leave to a manual build. Turn it on once, and every new subscription-form signup gets a confirmation email automatically, no journey to assemble. The trade-off is that it's one setting for the whole project: a single confirmation template, shared across every form on the account.

### Dormant at launch, and everything downstream waits with it

Set the SDK to start dormant, and it holds off on collecting or sending data at all, before a user has agreed to anything. Once consent comes in, one call flips it on and the same session picks up from there, without a reinstall or a fresh init: `startServerCommunication` on iOS and Android, `SetCommunicationEnabled` on Unity, `setCommunicationEnabled` on Web.

## Why it has to cover every channel

A consent gate that only reaches one channel isn't much of a gate. Push, email, in-app, and SMS all read from the same unified customer profile, so the SDK's dormant state holds back what every one of them would otherwise collect, not just the channel you had in mind when you called it. Certifications and hosting cover the infrastructure underneath: [SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001:2022, GDPR](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/data-safety/). This is the setting that decides whether a device's data reaches that infrastructure in the first place.

## How it works

**Set the SDK to start dormant**

Add the platform's off-by-default config ahead of your own consent screen: an Info.plist key on iOS, a manifest flag on Android and Unity, an init parameter on Web. It holds every SDK-driven collection and send until you turn it on.

**Turn on double opt-in for subscription forms**

On the Subscription forms page, enable the toggle and fill in the shared confirmation template once. Every new form signup then gets a confirmation email with a 24-hour link before it counts as consented.

**Enable the SDK when consent lands, or revoke it**

Once a user agrees, call the platform's enable method and collection resumes. If they withdraw consent later, the same call in reverse puts it right back to sleep.

## How it works with the rest

The gate decides whether data flows at all. Once it's open, [Tags](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/cdp-tags/) and [Events](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/user-events/) are what that data becomes on the user's profile, and a [Message preset](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/message-presets/) is what actually gets sent once someone is reachable. Q: What is a customer journey for e-commerce?

A: A customer journey for e-commerce is the complete path a shopper takes from first discovering your brand to becoming a loyal repeat customer. It includes awareness (ads, search, social), consideration (browsing products, reading reviews), purchase (adding to cart, checkout), and post-purchase stages (order updates, reviews, repeat purchases).\n\nPushwoosh Customer Journey Builder lets you visualize these stages and automate messaging at each touchpoint. Instead of sending one-off campaigns, you create connected sequences that guide customers through their shopping journey with the right message at the right time.

Q: How does customer journey automation reduce cart abandonment?

A: Customer journey automation addresses cart abandonment by creating multi-touch recovery sequences that reach shoppers through multiple channels with escalating urgency.\n\nWith Pushwoosh, you can build a journey that starts with an in-app message while the shopper is still browsing, sends a push notification reminder an hour later, and follows up with an email the next day featuring the abandoned items and a discount code. Drop a Reachability check element between steps, and the journey automatically falls back to the next channel — push, then email, then SMS — for shoppers who aren't reachable on the first one, instead of silently losing them.\n\nUnlike single-message campaigns, automated journeys adapt based on customer response. If someone opens the push notification but doesn't purchase, they continue to the email step. If they complete the purchase, they exit the recovery journey and enter a post-purchase sequence instead. This intelligent orchestration recovers significantly more abandoned carts than manual campaigns.

Q: What e-commerce events can trigger customer journeys?

A: Pushwoosh supports triggering customer journeys from any e-commerce event you track. Common triggers include cart events (add to cart, remove from cart, cart abandonment), purchase events (first purchase, repeat purchase, high-value order), browse events (product viewed, category browsed, search performed), and engagement events (app open, push notification opened, email clicked).\n\nYou can also trigger journeys based on the absence of events. For example, start a re-engagement journey for customers who haven't made a purchase in 30 days, or send browse abandonment messages to shoppers who viewed products but didn't add anything to cart.\n\nCustom events specific to your business, such as loyalty points earned, wishlist additions, or store locator searches, can also trigger journeys.

Q: How does RFM segmentation work for e-commerce customer journeys?

A: RFM segmentation categorizes customers based on Recency (when they last purchased), Frequency (how often they purchase), and Monetary value (how much they spend). Pushwoosh automatically calculates RFM scores and places customers into segments like Champions, Loyal Customers, At-Risk, and Lost.\n\nEach segment receives different customer journeys. Champions might get early access to sales and exclusive products. At-Risk customers receive win-back campaigns with personalized incentives based on their purchase history. Lost customers enter reactivation journeys with stronger offers.\n\nAs customers' behavior changes, they automatically move between segments and transition into the appropriate journey. This ensures every customer receives messaging that matches their relationship with your brand.

Q: Can I personalize customer journey messages with product data?

None of that survives the tap. Rebuilding that path by hand, in every message, is the kind of work that gets skipped under deadline, so it usually is. Deep links and custom data carry the destination and the payload inside the message itself, so the tap lands where the message promised.

## What it does

A message preset can carry two things beyond its text: a deep link URI and a block of custom data. The URI accepts `` tokens, filled in per recipient from segment or event attributes, so one template can point at a different product page, match lobby or order for each person it reaches. Custom data travels as JSON in the message payload, under the key `u`, for your app to read and act on after the tap.

| Setting | What it carries | Where it's set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deep link URI | Custom URI scheme with  tokens filled per recipient | Message preset |
| Custom data | JSON payload delivered under the key u | Message preset |
| Also available via | The journey's Data to App element, with no push attached | Customer Journey Builder |

Both belong to the preset itself. Every campaign, journey step and API call built from that preset opens the same place with the same data, without re-entering either one.

### One template, a different screen for each recipient

The URI template stays fixed on the preset; only the placeholder value changes per person. That's what lets a single cart-abandonment preset open a different product page for every recipient, instead of every abandoned-cart message needing its own hand-built link.

## Why Customer Journey Builder needs this

A journey can decide who gets a message and when, but not what happens after the tap, unless the message itself carries that instruction. Without a deep link, a step that fires on an abandoned cart still opens the app's home screen, and the person has to re-find the cart on their own, if they bother. Deep links and custom data are what let [Customer Journey Builder](https://www.pushwoosh.com/products/customer-journey/) finish the job a trigger started, instead of stopping at the notification.

Q: What is first purchase onboarding and why does it matter for e-commerce?

A: First purchase onboarding is a structured communication sequence that guides new customers through the period immediately following their initial purchase. It typically includes order confirmation, product education, brand storytelling, loyalty program introductions, and personalized recommendations for complementary products.\n\nThis period is critical for e-commerce brands because it determines whether a first-time buyer becomes a repeat customer or never returns. Research shows that acquiring a new customer costs 5-7 times more than retaining an existing one, yet many brands invest heavily in acquisition while neglecting the post-purchase experience.\n\nWith Pushwoosh, you can automate the entire first purchase onboarding journey across push notifications, email, in-app messages, and SMS. Automated onboarding campaigns reach new buyers at the right moment with the right content, building the trust and engagement needed to drive repeat purchases.

Q: How does automated first purchase onboarding work in Pushwoosh?

A: Pushwoosh detects when a customer completes their first purchase by tracking the purchase event from your e-commerce app or website. This event triggers an automated onboarding journey built in Customer Journey Builder.\n\nA typical first purchase onboarding flow starts with an immediate thank-you message, followed by product tips or care instructions 24-48 hours later. Over the next 1-2 weeks, the sequence delivers brand education, loyalty program invitations, and personalized product recommendations based on what the customer purchased.\n\nEach message adapts to customer behavior in real time. If a new buyer opens a product education email and clicks through, the next message can be a cross-sell recommendation. If they go inactive, the journey can trigger a re-engagement offer. The entire flow runs automatically once configured, onboarding every new customer 24/7 without manual intervention.

Q: What channels can I use for first purchase onboarding?

A: Pushwoosh supports first purchase onboarding across multiple channels: push notifications, in-app messages, email, SMS, and WhatsApp. You can use any combination of these channels in a single onboarding flow.\n\nPush notifications work well for quick touchpoints like order updates and product tips. In-app messages are effective for showcasing loyalty programs or product tutorials when the customer is actively browsing. Email provides a richer format for detailed product education and brand storytelling. SMS and WhatsApp deliver high open rates for time-sensitive offers like expiring discounts.\n\nThe most effective onboarding approach uses multiple channels in a coordinated sequence. For example: a push notification thanking the customer right after purchase, a product education email at 48 hours, an in-app loyalty program invitation on next app open, and a cross-sell recommendation push at 7 days. Pushwoosh manages channel coordination automatically so customers never receive conflicting or duplicate messages.

Q: How can I personalize the onboarding experience for different customer segments?

A: Pushwoosh enables granular segmentation of new buyers based on multiple criteria:\n\n**Purchase value**: Create different onboarding flows for high-value first purchases (premium content, concierge-style messaging) versus entry-level purchases (product discovery, value reinforcement).\n\n**Product category**: Tailor onboarding content to what the customer bought. A new skincare buyer gets a skincare routine guide; a new electronics buyer gets setup tutorials and accessory recommendations.\n\n**Acquisition source**: Customize messaging based on how the customer found you. Customers from paid ads may need more brand education, while organic visitors may already be familiar with your products.\n\n**Engagement behavior**: Adapt the journey based on how the customer interacts with onboarding messages. Active engagers can receive more frequent touchpoints, while quieter customers get a lighter sequence to avoid fatigue.\n\nAll segments update in real time as customer behavior changes, ensuring each new buyer receives the onboarding approach most likely to drive their second purchase.

You can use these insights to continuously optimize your onboarding flows and maximize the lifetime value of every new customer.

Q: When should I start sending onboarding messages after a first purchase?

A: The optimal timing for first purchase onboarding depends on your product category and delivery timeline, but the general principle is to start immediately and maintain momentum.\n\nSend the first message (thank you and order confirmation) right after purchase. Follow up with product education or brand content 24-48 hours later, while the customer is still excited about their order. If your product requires delivery, use the waiting period to build anticipation with shipping updates and product tips.\n\nAfter the customer receives their order, send usage guides or care instructions within 1-2 days.
